facts.text: Note on the name: the canonical object is a **single** aggregation stage, `$emit`. The plural "operators" is best read as covering its six connection-type syntax variants (Kafka, Atlas time series, Kinesis, S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Pub/Sub), each of which takes a different field set. There is no family of separately named `$emit*` operators.

**A2.** The single-`$emit` rule means fan-out to multiple sinks is impossible within one stream processor. A pipeline that must write to both a Kafka topic and an S3 bucket requires two stream processors reading the same source, which doubles source consumption and breaks any shared exactly-once framing. This is a direct consequence of A1 and the identical constraint on `$merge` ("`$merge` must be the last stage of any pipeline it appears in. You can use only one `$merge` stage per pipeline") — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-merge/>
**Q9. Why the stage is called `$emit` is unattested.** The map-reduce `emit()` connection is an observation about MongoDB's own vocabulary, not a documented lineage. [H-D5]

A reader who assumes `$emit` is generally available in the aggregation framework is wrong. — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/> [history 3] - The plural "operators" denotes **one** stage with six connection-type syntax variants, n

You can use only one `$emit` stage per pipeline." — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-emit/>

This report covers only the `$emit` aggregation stage of MongoDB Atlas Stream Processing: what it is, its parts, its per-destination field contracts, the invariants it enforces, and its stated limits. It does not cover `$source`, windowing stages, `$merge` internals, the connection registry, or Atlas Stream Processing operations — those are separate frontier items. `$merge` appears only where the `$emit` contract is defined by contrast with it.

**D4.** Apache Kafka 4.0 defaults `enable.idempotence` to `true` — <https://kafka.apache.org/40/generated/producer_config.html>. ASP does not expose `enable.idempotence` in `$emit.config`; the documented `config` keys are `acks`, `compression_type`, `dateFormat`, `headers`, `key`, `keyFormat`, `outputFormat`, `tombstoneWhen` — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-emit/>. Whether ASP's internal producer enables idempotence, and what it does when a user sets `acks: "0"` (which is incompatible with idempotent production in stock Kafka), is not stated — see *Unresolve

**H2.** `$emit` to Kafka could hang indefinitely under producer backpressure. The 23 October 2024 release "Ensures calls to produce messages to Apache Kafka don't hang indefinitely, even when the producer queue is full." — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/changelog/> **Consequence:** the existence of this fix confirms that a saturated downstream Kafka cluster could stall an ASP pipeline with no timeout. The changelog does not state the timeout value now applied or what happens to in-flight messages when it fires.

This report covers only the `$emit` aggregation stage as defined by MongoDB Atlas Stream Processing (ASP): what it is, when it appeared, and how its surface area grew over time. Sibling ASP stages (`$merge`, `$source`, `$https`, `$iceberg`, `$externalFunction`), the ASP product as a whole, and the MongoDB Server aggregation framework are referenced only where they fix `$emit`'s boundaries. They are not researched here.

7. **2 May 2024** — general availability, announced at MongoDB `.local` NYC. — https://www.infoworld.com/article/2337054/mongodb-atlas-stream-processing-is-finally-here.html The GA post records two `$emit`-relevant additions: emitting processor results into **time series collections** ("Pre-process data continuously while saving it for historical access later"), and **Kafka header** support. It also flags "additional data sources and sinks" beyond Kafka and Atlas databases as roadmap. — https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/product-release-announcements/atlas-stream-processing-now-generally-ava

12. **18 August 2025** — `$emit` gains `config.tombstoneWhen` (a boolean expression): when it evaluates true, `$emit` sends a `null` value, so a stream processor can drive **Kafka topic compaction**. This is the most semantically significant post-GA addition — before it, `$emit` could only append, never signal deletion.

16. `config.tombstoneWhen` takes a boolean expression; when it evaluates true, `$emit` writes a `null` value to the Kafka topic. This exists specifically to let a stream processor participate in Kafka log compaction, which uses null values as delete tombstones. It was added in the 18 August 2025 release. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/changelog/

**S25.** `config.tombstoneWhen` takes a boolean expression; when true, `$emit` writes a `null` value to the Kafka topic, letting a stream processor drive Kafka log compaction. Added in the 18 August 2025 release. History rates it "the most semantically significant post-GA addition — before it, `$emit` could only append, never signal deletion." — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/changelog/> (4/4: M16, H12, E-B5, P13). Topic compaction via `tombstoneWhen` requires `key` and `keyFormat`. [H18]

**E3.** Time series `$emit` has a much tighter, separately stated ceiling: "The maximum size for documents within a time series collection is 4 MB." — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-emit/>

**H1.** The Kafka `$emit` sink buffered output for a full second until early 2025. The 14 January 2025 release "Changes the buffering duration for `$emit` Aggregation Stage (Stream Processing) to Apache Kafka sinks from 1000 milliseconds to five milliseconds." — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/changelog/> **Consequence:** any latency benchmark, blog post, or architecture decision about ASP Kafka sinks dated before 2025-01-14 reflects a 200× larger sink buffer and should not be trusted for current latency claims.

**H4.** S3 and Azure `$emit` flush on whichever of three thresholds fires first — `writeOptions.count`, `writeOptions.bytes` (default 32 MB), or `writeOptions.interval` (default 1 minute, maximum 7 days). — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-emit/> **Boundary condition:** a low-volume stream with defaults produces a file per minute regardless of how few records it holds, which is a small-file problem for downstream analytics; raising `interval` toward the 7-day maximum trades that for a 7-day visibility lag on the sink.
10. **14 January 2025** — buffering duration for `$emit` to Apache Kafka sinks cut from 1000 ms to **five milliseconds**. This is the clearest latency-oriented change in `$emit`'s history.
21. Documents written to a MongoDB time series collection via `$emit` are capped at 4 MB. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-emit/

This matters directly for object-store destinations, where `writeOptions` may hold up to 32 MB or one minute of data in a buffer that could span a checkpoint boundary. No source found resolves it. This report covers the `$emit` aggregation stage of MongoDB Atlas Stream Processing (ASP) only: its sink variants, configuration surface, operational behaviour, failure modes, and the trade-offs of choosing it. "Operators" here means the family of `$emit` forms — one per supported sink connection type — plus the config sub-operators (`key`, `keyFormat`, `tombstoneWhen`, `outputFormat`, `dateFormat`, `partitionBy`, `writeOptions`, `parallelism`).

**S45. Failure mode — unrecoverable checkpoint, lossy restart.** "If the oplog resume token that Atlas Stream Processing stored in the last checkpoint is no longer in the source cluster's oplog when you restart the processor, Atlas Stream Processing cannot resume from that checkpoint. To recover, restart the processor with `resumeFromCheckpoint=false`." The sink loses the messages that fell in the gap. — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/architecture/> (2/4: M25, E-D7)

**A3.** `$emit` and `$merge` are not interchangeable, and each has a target class the other cannot reach. `$merge` writes to ordinary Atlas collections; `$emit` is the only stage that writes to Atlas time series collections. Exact wording: "`$merge` can't write to time series collections. To write documents to time series collections, use the `$emit` stage." — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-merge/>

**B5.** `config.tombstoneWhen` (Kafka) is a per-message expression that emits a `null` value for log compaction. If it fails to evaluate, the document goes to the DLQ. The operations guide lists this as a *common* processing error, naming the exact trigger: "Your pipeline includes the `$emit.config.tombstoneWhen` configuration field to delete Kafka records and a given document is missing the field to be evaluated." — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/ops-guide/> **Failure mode:** a sparse or optional field in `tombstoneWhen` sends *every* document lacking that field t

**C2.** **Disconfirming evidence.** That statement holds only where the broker has `auto.create.topics.enable=true`. On Confluent Cloud the setting defaults to `false` and is editable *only* on Dedicated clusters: "Automatic topic creation (`auto.create.topics.enable`) is disabled by default (`false`) to help prevent unexpected costs," and "You cannot edit cluster settings on Basic, Standard, Enterprise, and Freight clusters in Confluent Cloud." — <https://docs.confluent.io/cloud/current/clusters/broker-config.html> **Failure mode:** on any Confluent Cloud Basic/Standard/Enterprise/Freight clu

**D2.** Setting `config.acks: "0"` makes `$emit` a fire-and-forget sink with no delivery guarantee and no DLQ recourse, because the failure is never observed. Apache Kafka: with `acks=0` "the producer will not wait for any acknowledgment from the server at all. The record will be immediately added to the socket buffer and considered sent." — <https://kafka.apache.org/40/generated/producer_config.html> **Boundary condition:** the DLQ catches *processing* errors (parse failures, expression failures, key generation, oversize records — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/op

**D6.** Modifying a windowed pipeline compounds D5: "Processors with windows may reprocess some data as a product of recalculating the windows," and modified processors restore from the last checkpoint by default (`resumeFromCheckpoint=true`). — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/manage-stream-processor/> **Failure mode:** editing a pipeline's non-window stages can still cause the window to re-emit aggregates already written by `$emit`, producing duplicate or superseding records downstream with no version marker to distinguish them.

**D7.** Checkpoint resume can become impossible for change-stream sources, forcing a lossy restart that also affects `$emit` output continuity: "If the oplog resume token that Atlas Stream Processing stored in the last checkpoint is no longer in the source cluster's oplog when you restart the processor, Atlas Stream Processing cannot resume from that checkpoint. To recover, restart the processor with `resumeFromCheckpoint=false`." — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/architecture/>

**E1.** The `$emit` reference states a 16 MB default with a conditional increase: "Atlas Stream Processing doesn't support writing BSON documents larger than `16MB` with the `$emit` stage to an AWS or Azure blob storage sink. You can increase this limit to up to `125MB` if your stream processor's source isn't a MongoDB deployment, or if earlier pipeline stages such as `$lookup` increase the size of your documents." — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-emit/>

**E2.** **Contradicting statement on MongoDB's own Limitations page**, which reports only the ceiling, drops the 16 MB default, drops the conditions, and narrows the scope to S3: "Atlas Stream Processing doesn't support writing BSON documents larger than `125 MB` using the `$emit` stage to an AWS S3 bucket." — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/limitations/> **Consequence:** a reader who sizes capacity from the Limitations page will believe documents up to 125 MB always pass, when the reference page says the effective limit is 16 MB unless specific conditions hold, and

**U1. Behaviour at the 1000 dynamic-expression ceiling is undefined in the documentation.** The changelog records the limit's increase to 1000 — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/changelog/> — but the `$emit` reference never mentions it, and no source states whether the 1001st distinct target produces a processor error, a DLQ entry, a silent drop, or LRU eviction of an existing target. This is the single largest unknown for high-cardinality routing designs.

**U7. Independent verification is effectively absent.** No third-party benchmark, post-mortem, or peer-reviewed evaluation of `$emit` was located. The only non-MongoDB, non-Kafka source found that discusses `$emit` directly — a 2026-03-31 tutorial by Nawaz Dhandala — shows only a two-field example (`connectionName`, `topic`) and covers none of `key`, `keyFormat`, `headers`, topic creation, error handling, or operational caveats. — <https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-31-mongodb-connect-atlas-stream-processing-kafka/view>. Every behavioural claim in sections A, B, E, F, G, and H therefore r

**Caveat on independence.** The gate is met on host count and on the presence of disconfirming evidence, but not on behavioural independence. No source outside MongoDB was found that empirically tests `$emit` behaviour. Apache Kafka and Confluent documentation constrain what `$emit` *can* do at the broker boundary; they say nothing about what ASP actually does inside that boundary. Claims in sections A, B, E, F, G, and H should be treated as vendor assertions pending empirical test, and U1–U4 are answerable only by running a processor.

4. The name echoes, but is unrelated to, the `emit()` key/value function of MongoDB map-reduce. Map-reduce has been deprecated since MongoDB 5.0 in favour of aggregation pipelines. No lineage between the two constructs is documented in any source found. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/map-reduce/

9. **11 October 2024** — two direct `$emit` changes: support for the `compression.type` and `acks` settings in the Apache Kafka `$emit` configuration; and the `$emit`/`$merge` dynamic expression limit raised to `1000`.

**Caveat on gate quality:** the evolution timeline (claims 8–16) rests almost entirely on a single document — MongoDB's official ASP changelog. That is the appropriate primary source, but it is not independently corroborated. No third-party source found tracks `$emit`'s per-release changes.

13. The number of distinct dynamic targets a processor may fan out to is bounded. The 11 October 2024 release increased the `$emit` and `$merge` dynamic expression limit to 1000. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/changelog/

22. Object-store writes have a 16 MB default document limit, extensible to 125 MB when the source is not MongoDB or when earlier pipeline stages such as `$lookup` have grown the document. The hard ceiling is stated as a product limitation: "Atlas Stream Processing doesn't support writing BSON documents larger than `125 MB` using the `$emit` stage to an AWS S3 bucket." — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/limitations/ and https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-emit/

23. **Delivery semantics are a limit on `$emit`, not a guarantee it provides.** Atlas Stream Processing guarantees at-least-once processing. Checkpoints record source offsets — oplog resume tokens for change streams, partition offsets for Kafka — not copies of documents, and a restarted or failed-over processor reprocesses everything since the last checkpoint. Consequently `$emit` can write the same message to its sink more than once, and downstream consumers must tolerate duplicates. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/architecture/

The caveat: `$emit` is a proprietary feature of a single vendor's managed service, so there is no standards body, no independent implementation, and no peer-reviewed literature against which to check it. All mechanism-level claims (4–25) trace to MongoDB's own documentation. The independent sources corroborate the stage's role and basic syntax; none of them independently verifies the field tables, the limits, or the delivery semantics. Treat those as vendor-asserted, not independently confirmed.

This synthesis covers the `$emit` aggregation stage of Atlas Stream Processing and nothing else: its parts, its six per-destination field contracts, its invariants, its documented limits, its dated evolution, and its failure modes. `$merge`, `$source`, `$https`, `$iceberg`, `$externalFunction`, windowing, the Connection Registry, tiering, and ASP as a product appear only where they fix `$emit`'s boundary or determine whether an `$emit` succeeds.

**S3.** `$merge` cannot write to time series collections, so `$emit` is the only sink route to an Atlas time series collection — inverting the intuition that `$merge` owns Atlas targets. Exact wording: "`$merge` can't write to time series collections. To write documents to time series collections, use the `$emit` stage." — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-merge/> (3/4: M4, E-A3, P3)

**S19.** The number of distinct dynamic targets is bounded at 1000, raised to that figure in the 11 October 2024 release. — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/changelog/> (3/4: M13, H9, E-B3) — **edge-cases adds the sharper framing: the limit appears only in the changelog and is absent from the `$emit` reference page, so a pipeline can pass review against the reference and still hit the ceiling in production.** [E-B3]

**S26. Failure mode — `tombstoneWhen` over a sparse field.** The operations guide lists this as a *common* processing error, naming the exact trigger: "Your pipeline includes the `$emit.config.tombstoneWhen` configuration field to delete Kafka records and a given document is missing the field to be evaluated." A sparse or optional field in `tombstoneWhen` therefore sends *every* document lacking that field to the DLQ, not only the ones intended as tombstones. — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/ops-guide/> [E-B5, P34] (2/4)

**S34.** Cumulative parallelism is `parallelism_total - parallelized_stages`, where `parallelism_total` sums all `parallelism` values greater than 1 across `$source`, `$lookup`, `$merge`, `$emit`, and `$externalFunction`, capped by stream processor tier. Exceeding the budget is a hard failure at definition time, not a degradation: "If a stream processor exceeds the maximum cumulative parallelism for its tier, Atlas Stream Processing throws an error and advises you of the minimum processor tier required for your intended level of parallelism." — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-

**S46. Failure mode — editing a windowed pipeline re-emits.** "Processors with windows may reprocess some data as a product of recalculating the windows," and modified processors restore from the last checkpoint by default (`resumeFromCheckpoint=true`). Editing a pipeline's *non-window* stages can therefore cause the window to re-emit aggregates `$emit` already wrote, producing duplicate or superseding records downstream with no version marker to distinguish them. — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/manage-stream-processor/> [E-D6] (1/4)

**S48. Sink choice forfeits failover.** Failover processors support only Atlas and Apache Kafka sinks and require tier SP10 or higher — so S3, Kinesis, Azure Blob, and Pub/Sub `$emit` targets cannot be used with failover at all. — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/limitations/> [P39] (1/4 — one of the highest-value single-report findings in the set; it constrains sink selection before any performance consideration)

This report covers only the `$emit` aggregation stage of MongoDB Atlas Stream Processing (ASP) — the sink stage that writes a stream processor's output to an external target. It covers all six documented `$emit` connection variants: Apache Kafka, Atlas time series collections, AWS Kinesis, AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, and Google Cloud Pub/Sub.

**Evidence base:** official MongoDB documentation (primary, but vendor-authored), the Apache Kafka standard, Confluent Cloud operational documentation, and one third-party tutorial. No independent benchmark, incident report, or peer-reviewed study of `$emit` was found — see *Quality Gate* below.

**G1.** `parallelism` on `$emit` is not free capacity; it is drawn from a per-tier budget shared with other stages. The cumulative figure is "`parallelism total - parallelized stages`", where `parallelism total` sums all `parallelism` values greater than 1 across `$source`, `$lookup`, `$merge`, `$emit`, and `$externalFunction`. — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-emit/>

**G3.** Azure Blob Storage `$emit` caps `parallelism` at 16; S3 and time series state only that the maximum "depends on stream processor tier". — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-emit/>

**G5.** Everything outside the parallelizable stages is single-threaded: "Atlas Stream Processing uses a single core for transformation pipeline stages, except for stages that can specify a `parallelism` value." — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/limitations/>. Raising `$emit.parallelism` does not relieve an upstream transformation bottleneck.

**S27.** `$emit` supports a Schema Registry for Kafka output via `schemaRegistry`, with `valueSchema.type`, `valueSchema.schema` (an Avro Schema Declaration), and options `autoRegisterSchemas` (default `true`) and `subjectNameStrategy` (`TopicNameStrategy` default, `RecordNameStrategy`, `TopicRecordNameStrategy`). Avro is the only serialization type currently supported here. — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-emit/> (3/4: M17, H14, P16)

**S30.** ASP's Kafka connectivity supports only the `SASL_PLAINTEXT`, `SASL_SSL`, and `SSL` security protocols, which constrains which brokers `$emit` can reach at all. — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/limitations/> [E-C3] (1/4)

**S36.** Raising `$emit.parallelism` does not relieve an upstream bottleneck: "Atlas Stream Processing uses a single core for transformation pipeline stages, except for stages that can specify a `parallelism` value." — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/limitations/> [E-G5] (1/4)

**S42.** ASP guarantees **at-least-once** processing and nothing stronger. No exactly-once claim for `$emit` was found on any page examined by any of the four reports. Documents may be emitted more than once, particularly during initial sync; downstream consumers must be idempotent or tolerate duplicates. — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/limitations/> and <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/architecture/> (3/4: M23, E-D5, P37)

**Side A — the changelog** names the setting `compression.type` (dotted, matching the Apache Kafka producer property). — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/changelog/> **Side B — the `$emit` reference** documents it as `config.compression_type` (underscored). — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/sp-agg-emit/>

The changelog records Kinesis as `$source` and `$emit` sink on **3 December 2025**, then records "support for AWS Kinesis connections as source and sink options" again on **16 February 2026**. No source says whether the second entry is the Atlas UI / connection-registry exposure of an already-shipped capability or a separate GA step. — <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/changelog/> [H-D3] (1/4; the other three reports cite only 3 Dec 2025)

**Side A — the narrow framing.** Independent write-ups characterize `$emit` as the Kafka-topic sink and `$merge` as the MongoDB sink. — <https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-31-mongodb-how-to-write-stream-processing-pipelines-in-mongodb-atlas/view>, <https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-31-mongodb-connect-atlas-stream-processing-kafka/view>

Three reports [M2, H2, P2] carry the overview page's claim that `$emit` and `$merge` are ASP's **two** sink stages, mutually exclusive, one per processor. The changelog records two further terminal stages since: `$https` as "an alternative final stage" (7 January 2026) and `$iceberg` at GA as "a separate terminal stage" (30 June 2026). [H14, H16]

history draws half of this conclusion — "`$emit` is therefore no longer ASP's only non-`$merge` terminal stage" [H16] — but does not carry it back to the overview claim the other three reports repeated as current. **Consequence: the "two sink stages" framing, which every report treats as settled background, appears to be as stale as the "`$emit` is the Kafka sink" framing in X7, and from the same page.** The mutual-exclusivity rule's status with respect to `$https` and `$iceberg` is not stated anywhere located. Unresolved.

**Q2. Producer idempotence is unaddressed.** Apache Kafka 4.0 defaults `enable.idempotence` to `true` (<https://kafka.apache.org/40/generated/producer_config.html>) and stock Kafka rejects idempotence combined with `acks=0`. ASP does not expose `enable.idempotence` in `$emit.config` (documented keys: `acks`, `compression_type`, `dateFormat`, `headers`, `key`, `keyFormat`, `outputFormat`, `tombstoneWhen`) yet permits `config.acks: "0"`, without saying whether it disables idempotence, errors, or silently overrides. No MongoDB page located addresses ASP producer idempotence at all. [E-D4, E-U2]

**Q8. No dated first appearance of the `$emit` token.** The earliest dated source naming `$emit` is the 13 February 2024 public-preview post. `$emit` clearly existed during the June 2023–February 2024 private preview, but no public, dated primary source from that window was found. [H-D4]

**Q10. Vendor performance and cost claims are unverified, and the null result is the finding.** MongoDB argues `$emit`/`$merge` inside ASP replaces Kafka Connect connectors, claiming per-SPI-worker pricing (up to four stream processors per worker) beats per-task pricing from hosted Kafka providers, and that early customers found ASP "more performant than similar data movement in their Kafka Connector configurations" — published 9 September 2024, updated 6 March 2025, **with no published benchmark**. — <https://www.mongodb.com/blog/post/atlas-stream-processing-cost-effective-way-integrate-kafka
**Q11. No independent empirical verification of `$emit` exists at all.** All four reports reach this conclusion separately — see the saturation verdict.

**Evidence of saturation.** Four independent research passes, run the same day with no shared intermediate state, converged on the same claim set from the same small corpus. Nineteen distinct claims were recovered by all four passes independently (S1, S5, S9, S12, S14, S22, S25, S31, S33, S37, plus the 11 Oct 2024, 14 Jan 2025, 2 Jun 2025, 18 Aug 2025, 3 Dec 2025, 6 Apr 2026, and 15 Apr 2026 changelog entries). Every pass reached the same three headline conclusions: `$emit` is a single terminal stage with six per-sink variants; dynamic routing with no DLQ loses data silently; the delivery guar

The one genuine exception is edge-cases' use of `kafka.apache.org` and `docs.confluent.io` — and those sources constrain only what `$emit` *can* do at the broker boundary; they say nothing about what ASP does inside it. That single move is nonetheless what produced X2, the most production-consequential finding in the whole set, which suggests the productive remaining direction is **more boundary standards, not more MongoDB pages**.
